utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Domazet: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. VGD22, good morning. We shall continue our conversation that we started yesterday afternoon when you explained how and when you saw Mitar Vasiljevic near your house as you were on your way home. Did you ever see him in the command for which you provided security at Bikavac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. I understand where we're going to pick up from. The only problem is my monitor's not switched on, so I can't follow the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So your question was whether I ever saw Mr. Vasiljevic at the command where I worked in the security.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to see Mr. Vasiljevic at the command which I provided security for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of him coming to the command at Bikavac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My colleagues who were working in the security at the command told me on one occasion that he had come to the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find out what the reason was for his coming and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why he came, but I think a misunderstanding occurred in the command. I think that Mr. Vasiljevic had, I think, refused to carry out an order of the command, and I think he left his weapon at the command and marched out in a huff. At least that is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, you learned from others, because you were not at the command at the time, Mr. Vasiljevic came, there was a discussion, and you said he left his weapon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with Mr. Vasiljevic after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I was working in the security of the command, I know that they took Mr. Vasiljevic into custody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Vasiljevic taken into custody at the command itself or was it somewhere else? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was at the command itself or at some other place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this detention that Mr. Vasiljevic was taken to, as you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I don't recall there being any challenge to your client's evidence about this. If there is something that you really want him to deal with, I suggest you lead him to the position where you want him to add something to what's already been said. I know you're being very careful to not ask leading questions, but there was no issue taken that your client was charged with something, and indeed there is some promise, I think it was by you, that you would produce the document indicating what the punishment was. So if you want this witness to deal with something, please take him to it. It will save us an awful lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately, we do not have any document about this - Mr. Vasiljevic testified to that - nor do we have a document in our possession today about his detention. That is why I address these questions to this witness. But I shall try and limit myself to what may be of importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my next question would be whether you had occasion to see Mr. Vasiljevic during the time he was in prison.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once I did have occasion to see him in the prison where he was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe how that happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, the encounter occurred as follows: My neighbour and friend, Dr. Radomir Vasiljevic, had been informed that Mr. Mitar was in detention, and since he knew that I was on duty in the security of the command, he asked me whether I could go with him to the place where the detention unit was, for us to be able to visit Mitar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else go with you in addition to Dr. Radomir Vasiljevic and yourself, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it's been a long time, I think that we used the ambulance to go to the detention unit, and I assume that one of the nurses may have been present in the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from Dr. Vasiljevic, or anyone else, the reason why the doctor and possibly a nurse needed to visit him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radomir Vasiljevic had been informed that Mr. Mitar was refusing food in detention, that he refused to eat, and he went to check that out, to see whether it was true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you personally see Mr. Vasiljevic, or was it only Dr. Radomir Vasiljevic who actually saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I also saw Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, or could you perhaps tell us approximately when that was when this happened, bearing in mind the time that you know you spent at Bikavac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean a date, then I would say it could have been the end of May, possibly the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long Mr. Vasiljevic was held in that detention unit, for how many days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how much time Mr. Vasiljevic was held there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, did you see him around in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shortly after that, shall I say a couple of days after this visit of ours, I would see Mr. Vasiljevic in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what he was doing when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see him -- or I saw him once when he was some kind of a monitor, a person working with a group of other people cleaning the streets and shop windows in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how he was dressed on that occasion, what kind of clothing he wore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, at the time Mr. Vasiljevic was dressed, in part, in military clothes, because I remember well he was just wearing SMB, or that is, olive-grey trousers of the former JNA, and on top he was wearing a civilian shirt or jacket of a darker colour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that he acted as a kind of monitor. How did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to that conclusion on the basis of two reasons. One was that I had heard from my colleagues previously that Mr. Vasiljevic was performing those duties, and the second reason was because - I don't remember now whether it was his left or his right arm - he was wearing a ribbon which was, in my mind, probably a marking for the Red Cross or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What colour was this ribbon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not quite sure, but I think it was red with white. Now, whether it was white with red or red with white, I'm not quite sure. I don't know which colour predominated. But it was an indication of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that in view of the colour that you remember the ribbon was in, that your association was that it was linked to the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he armed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion he certainly did not have a weapon. I didn't see a weapon on him. Because he himself participated in the cleaning of the streets and the shop windows. He was actually working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that after that day, you would also come across him. Was he armed on any of those other subsequent occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him as this monitor only once. The next time I would see him, it would be in front of his family home, and he was not armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when were you personally in Bikavac working as security of the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but very briefly. I performed those duties for a short while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I was assigned to the duty of an operator for ammunition, which actually I had done before the war had broken out, at the ammunition depot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you returned to (redacted) and continued working there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In that period of time, the (redacted) was not at (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After these occasions that you have described, when you saw Vasiljevic, did you continue seeing him in the course of June or July or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have seen him a couple of more times after that, but later, I was told that he was no longer in Visegrad, as he had an injury of his leg, a fracture of his leg, as I was told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear where he was undergoing treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the hospital in Uzice was where he was treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him after he returned from treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon his return from treatment, whenever I went home, I would see Mr. Vasiljevic in front of his own house. Usually he would be sitting there with a plaster cast on his leg. And if he was walking, he did so with the help of crutches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you lived quite close to his house and you knew him, could you tell us a few words about him as a person, especially what you knew about him in those days in particular.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I will manage to explain properly the person as I know him, for Mr. Vasiljevic, as far as his humane and moral qualities are concerned, was a positive character in every sense of the word. When I say "positive," I mean that there wasn't anyone who could say that he had done anything bad or that he had hurt anyone at all. Actually, there was no one who could say any such things. And I should like to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please try.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment I met Mr. Vasiljevic, as I lived in a certain family situation, he would always assist me. When I was building my own family house, in a period of time when the building was ongoing, I went to do my regular military service, and Mr. Vasiljevic, not only did he personally come to the assistance of my mother, as I was living with my mother only, but he also organised other neighbours and friends to lend a helping hand to my mother in the construction of our house. For me, this is a gesture that I will never forget. And there are other situations on the basis of which I see Mr. Vasiljevic as a noble and good-hearted man. I am married now and I have two children, a six-year-old daughter who is handicapped. She has been since she was two. And for a whole year, we chased around various medical institutions looking for remedies for my daughter. And among other things, on one occasion we needed to go to Italy for certain tests to be done over there. I think this was in 1998 or 1999. Mr. Vasiljevic, whenever we would meet, would inquire about my Tamara, my daughter, whether she was better. And when my wife was due to leave for Italy with Tamara, Mr. Vasiljevic came over and gave my wife a hundred German marks banknote, which was for us a lot of money in those days, for her to have on her journey. And for us, this was a lot of money, because our earnings were very small. And I considered this a most generous gesture which I will always remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this description. But let me ask you, in those days, in 1992, did you hear from others that Mr. Vasiljevic had done anything bad to anyone or that he was a member of any paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard from anyone that Mr. Vasiljevic was on bad terms with anyone. And if you were to ask anyone from Visegrad the same question, you would get the same answer. As regards paramilitary organisations and Mr. Vasiljevic's involvement with them, as far as I am familiar with the situation and as far as I know Mr. Vasiljevic, I cannot imagine him being one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you learnt that he was arrested and surrendered to the Detention Unit in The Hague, what was your reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, in view of the kind of person I know Mr. Vasiljevic to be, I was astonished that this could have happened to him, because I really couldn't think of a single reason that would justify him being held here as an accused for anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this just your opinion or was it shared by anyone else in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone was surprised that this should have happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Vasiljevic like to have a drink? And of course I mean spirits. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vasiljevic, in a certain period of his life, drank a little too much, which did not affect our good neighbourly relations. This applies both to me and other neighbours and acquaintances. Nor did it affect his family situation. What I mean to say is that the family did not suffer because he used alcohol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from this injury for which he was treated in hospital, as you explained, do you know whether he was injured at any other time after that again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vasiljevic did not seem to have any luck with those injuries. As soon as his plaster cast was taken off the first time he had broken his leg - I think he was visiting his father in the village - he broke the same leg again and had to go to Uzice for treatment once again, to the hospital there, and he had to wear a plaster cast for a long time again, so that was rather unlucky.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After what you have just told us about, was he injured at all? Did he have another incident of that kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do know that Mr. Vasiljevic had another spine operation during the war, and that operation was performed, I think, in Belgrade. After that, he had another injury. He was somewhere at the front lines, deployed there somewhere, and as far as I know, he wasn't very professional in handling weapons. He didn't -- and there was a self-inflicted injury that took place. He injured his foot. I don't remember whether it was the foot of the right or the left leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, I should like to ask you a few questions relating to the early period at the end of May, or rather, in April, when you were in (redacted), before the arrival of the Uzice Corps. Now, from the compound of your (redacted), was there shooting from there, before the Uzice Corps arrived, at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the (redacted), where I was working immediately prior to the outbreak of the war, quite certainly there was not. Not a single shot was fired. I'm quite sure about that. And let me explain. The first bullet that was fired, unintentionally, was by a member of the reserve forces from within the Uzice Corps, and this happened just by chance, and a fire broke out in one of the outhouses in the store house. I mention that because I know that that was the only bullet that caused problems for us in the warehouse itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as I understand you, this incident took place after the arrival of the Uzice Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said "not a single bullet." Now, to be precise, was there any shooting from a mortar or from any other type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From no kind of weapon was there any shooting from the (redacted), neither before the Uzice Corps arrived or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more question related to the departure of the Uzice Corps, which, as you said, took place in the days before the 19th of May. You said that the 19th of May was the date when the last members of the Uzice Corps left. Now, as they left Visegrad, did the members of the Uzice Corps take with them vehicles, armaments, and all the other equipment that they had with them, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I worked in the post that I did, I can say with full responsibility that after the departure of the Uzice Corps, everything in the warehouse was empty, and the doors were open, the keys were in the administrative building, and everything had been taken. It all went with the Uzice Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but what I was asking you was: Did they leave behind a tank, a top, or any other materiel of that kind, a gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't have materiel of that kind in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. VGD22. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to go, for a start, in a short private session because I have some questions which would reveal probably the identity of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are now back in public session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VGD22, you just told us at the end of your testimony today that Mitar Vasiljevic would have a drink from time to time; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you know, he continued regularly to work as a waiter; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He continued to build his new house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, he didn't react aggressively if drunk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He never behaved aggressively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Neither to you as a neighbour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards me as a neighbour, never. I don't know about -- and he wasn't aggressive to other neighbours either, and I said that he wasn't aggressive towards his family members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him drunk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to you, he never lost control, did he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Mitar Vasiljevic was convicted for having an altercation with a Serb in the 1980s?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us - and for the reference of the Court and the Defence, at transcript page 83 - that you were contracted by the JNA as of 1st of April, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not called. I signed a contract on permanent employment with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who negotiated this contract with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contract appeared in the Official Gazette. I responded to the competition that was published, and I had all the qualifications for that post and was accepted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get any support from any side, political support, for this position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by that. How do you mean "political support"? From what side? As I said --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had nothing to do with them, no contact with them at all. Not only with them but with no party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who paid your salaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the then-JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did your paycheques come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the command of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was the command of the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the army -- it was the army district in Sarajevo, and the command of the army was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you got your money from Belgrade; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went right to the (redacted) without any training, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but previously I had been trained for work of that kind, the work that I was later to do. I had been previously trained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where had you been trained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I did my regular military service in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you do your regular military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pec. It is a town in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VGD22, the JNA was a rather big army; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they did recruit you directly from Visegrad; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they recruit other people from Visegrad at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I can remember the names now, but when I responded to the competition and applied, they asked for five candidates. I think it was five, and I think that five were accepted for different work posts at the time. There were five vacancies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the five that were accepted, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All five were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from those five positions, did the JNA do any other recruitment at that time in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So later they did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would they recruit any paramilitaries as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all, by no means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you testified that you worked as an ammunition mechanic at the [redacted]. The (redacted) actually stored TO weapons ammunition for the whole municipality, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I am qualified enough to talk about that topic, but I think that they were federal reserves, federal ammunition reserves. And I would like to ask that as I still work in that work post in the same warehouse, that we do not discuss that portion of how much is where, whose it is, and so on. I'm thinking of the military materiel stored in that warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the witness has some serious concerns about his security, I would have a couple of questions to ask him about exactly the issue of weapons in storage, et cetera, and I would then ask to go for a short private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you any view on that, Mr. Domazet? It seems the witness does have some concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that we move into private session, because I feel that the witness is concerned. He's worried that the questions that might be asked of him might bring him into a difficult position and what was called in the JNA a military secret that he is obliged to keep, confidentiality and secrecy that he is obliged to keep. So I assume that the witness is concerned about that. But we can only know what that will entail when the question is actually asked. So I do agree that we go into private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer, we will go into private session and then I want to say something about what Mr. Domazet has said. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are now in public session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yesterday told us that at that time you feared an attack by Muslim extremists, and now you're telling us that you did have Muslim soldiers and co-workers at that time still with you. Wouldn't it have been logical to get rid of the Muslim soldiers first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To my understanding, that is not logical. When I said "Muslim extremists," not all the Muslim population was extremist, if I may say so, like those groups of extremists, and especially not professional military men. There were different ethnic groups, and especially those working in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if they would have feared an attack of their like, they would have not come to work any more, would they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As they said in those days, they were not their like. There was equal status for members of Serb and Muslim ethnicity that were working in the warehouse at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you, then, correctly, at that time there was no conflict between the Muslim and Serb population in Visegrad around the beginning of April; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Visegrad, yes, among the civilian population, but in the warehouse itself, amongst us, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the civilian population would fight with each other and the military would be peaceful; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they get their weapons from, the civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons were probably illegally procured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it rather correct, VGD22, that Serbs were provided, through political and military bodies, with weapons in spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I had no contact with weapons, I was not handling weapons, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon before 1st of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of April 1st, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of 1st of April, 1992, that was the beginning of my official contract with the JNA. Before that I was also in the (redacted), and both myself and all others were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question was: Did you have, before April 1st, 1992, a weapon? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means -- was there storage room for weapons if you would leave the (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The personal weapons we had would be left with the security of the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VGD22, it was wartime, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war could be said to have started on the 6th of April. You're asking me about the period prior to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then let's go after the 6th of April. You still worked at the (redacted); right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you say the war broke out on the 6th of April, it would have rather been unsafe to walk around without a weapon after that, no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that point in time, you didn't walk around without a weapon any more, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, too, I was in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also slept at the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not in the warehouse, but in a dormitory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when was the first time you personally would leave the (redacted) (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of May, when the JNA left the then Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you left the (redacted), would you take your weapon with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were all left with our personal weapons when the JNA left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that according to military rules, it would have been an offence to lose your weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, but I don't know which weapons were lost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally ever lose your weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume when you were on leave, you took it home with you, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I took it with me, but in most cases while we were at the warehouse, we left it there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking now after the warehouse, when you were basically assigned in Bikavac as a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was around end May; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that Mitar Vasiljevic was mobilised at the same time, correct, end May, 19th May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when he was mobilised, but he was mobilised, like everybody else who was able-bodied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew that he worked in a kitchen in Prelovo. You testified that at transcript page 94 of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he told you that he was a cook; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the assignments of a cook are actually to transport food back and forth from Visegrad front lines to supply food to soldiers and troops; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would have been rather unsafe for him to have no weapon; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't mean that the cook had to go personally every time distributing food to the troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's assume he would travel to Visegrad and back and forth. You would have taken along a weapon, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coming back to you, actually when you were assigned, how was your shift like in Bikavac? Did you work daytimes, night-times, mixed shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly they were day- and night-long shifts, so it depended on the time period how long our shifts would last.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would a usual -- how long would a usual shift last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think like guard duty. I don't think it lasted more than two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how often would you say you would go home, every two days, every day, every night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly how frequently we went home, but when I was free, when I was not on duty, I could be given a short leave to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went home, you took along your weapon, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not every time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Most of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that you never, ever, when you saw Mitar Vasiljevic, saw him with any kind of -- type of weapon; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason why Mitar Vasiljevic would tell us then that he possessed an automatic rifle during his time in Prelovo? You didn't see him with this, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see Mr. Vasiljevic mostly when he was on leave, in front of his house, and I never saw him when he was on duty as a cook in Prelovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't see him having an automatic rifle? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also never saw him carrying a submachine-gun, a so-called Schmeisser, in spring of 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once released from hospital in summer, you never saw him having a tommy submachine-gun in his house for his protection, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A Thompson gun, I think is the correct word. I'm sorry I confused you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So actually, you didn't saw him that often at all to be absolutely sure whether Mitar Vasiljevic had a gun or not; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As at the time he was on sick leave whenever I saw him in front of his house, he was not armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to see Mr. Vasiljevic cleaning the street. Did you see him once or several times doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a military policeman in the Bikavac Hotel, did you have any notice that Mitar Vasiljevic would undertake such a cleaning job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him, did you stop actually and talk to him or were you just in passing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you actually cannot really talk about the operation of the cleaning, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "in passing," I saw some people washing the shop windows, cleaning, removing certain posters and leaflets. Others were cleaning the streets with brooms. That is what I could see as I passed by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you passed by. Walking or in a car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, I was in an official vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So actually, you had just a short glimpse of Mr. Vasiljevic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way. I didn't stop the car. I didn't stop. I saw him from the car as I passed by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this was daytime or night-time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Daytime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people he was cleaning with were the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, there were both Serbs and Muslims. All the people who were employed in a particular shop would come out of the shop to clean their shop windows. The others were cleaning the streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was end May, beginning June of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the period, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Muslims were at war at that time with Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you explain the reason why Muslims would happily clean streets with a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, as would happen in my own unit, not all the people were keen on waging war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that most of the Muslim shops were actually closed at that time already?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified about Mitar Vasiljevic wearing a SMB old uniform. Did you ever see him with a black military-type hat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No such military hat exists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your testimony that in the whole military there was no military hat in existence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No black one, I think he's saying, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Black military hat. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no black hat among army members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what kind of colour hat, if any hat was worn by the military then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No hats were worn in the army as part of the official military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said as part of the "official military uniform." Were there unofficial occasions where a hat was worn?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Look, Ms. Bauer, I'm not sure where we're going with this. How can he answer that? A lot of people may have worn a military uniform and a black hat. How would he know, unofficially or otherwise? The problem is that the Prosecution seems to be unable to identify just what hat it is they're referring to. It's been described in other terms other than a military hat, and I don't really see that it is part of its case that the hat that the accused was seen wearing was any sort of military hat. It certainly hadn't been apparent if that is its case. So I don't see where you're getting with this cross-examination. If I may suggest that you move on to something that you may get somewhere with.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On his uniform -- you're a military person; right? You were a soldier.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were familiar with insignias; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the insignia you referred to Mitar Vasiljevic having was a Red Cross insignia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it was a mark indicating the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he wear this ribbon any time else apart from the one time you saw him cleaning the street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only then that I saw this ribbon on his arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you never, apart from this one time, saw him having this ribbon on the arm; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I saw him any other time with that ribbon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember having given a statement to Mr. Tanaskovic in August 1992 -- sorry, 2000.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you gave the statement voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you signed that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you signed it as basically true and accurate to your knowledge at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you say to Mr. Tanaskovic, and I quote you from the English translation: "I forgot to say that Mitar Vasiljevic wore an armband with a red cross on the said uniform. He also," and I stress the word "also," "wore that symbol when he was making the people clean the streets." Did you say that to Mr. Tanaskovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me, VGD22, that the word "also" refers that you have seen him more than once with the said Red Cross sign on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you see, the way I recollected that particular detail then, and I am reminded now again that he did have this red ribbon on his arm. It wasn't something that I would have to remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was rather such a distinct sign, wasn't it, that you refer to it as a Red Cross sign in the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, that it was a mark indicating affiliation with the Red Cross, because that type of work that he was doing was done by members of the Red Cross and the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever tell you that he worked for the Red Cross maybe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let me ask you: End May/beginning of June, you were to go to the town of Visegrad on occasions, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you see many Muslims around that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not many, but I would see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that most of them were leaving town in convoys at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. In that period I would still see them in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As part of the military police, did you ever arrest Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn that Muslim men were taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never heard that they were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer, may I remind you of something I said to Mr. Ossogo yesterday about this line of cross-examination. There was no dispute, as I understood it, to the Prosecution case that there was such conduct in relation to Muslims in this particular town or the area. Now, in those circumstances, do you need to pursue this witness' knowledge that it was going on if it's not in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not quite sure it's not in dispute, actually, because as far as I understood so far the Defence case, it still is in dispute that there was an attack on the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, there is on paper, but where was there in the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Well, so far we didn't hear all evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It was the obligation of the Defence to put its case to the Prosecution witnesses. None of them was cross-examined to suggest that their evidence in relation to that sort of thing was untrue. Now, the Trial Chamber is permitted in those circumstances to proceed upon the basis that it is not in issue. If the Defence is unwise enough to attempt to bring evidence in its case that it hasn't raised in the cross-examination of the Prosecution case, then you will have a case in reply. Let us not attempt to assume that the Defence doesn't know what it's doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VGD22, you told us something yesterday about the relocation of or dismantling of the (redacted). Where was the materiel relocated to, if you testified about relocation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the ammunition (redacted), already while the Uzice Corps was present there, was dislocated and moved to other warehouses outside Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VGD22, I'd like to go back to the Red Cross sign. I'd like to understand your testimony. Did you say today that you actually saw a Red Cross symbol or that you assume that Mitar Vasiljevic wore a Red Cross symbol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I saw Mitar Vasiljevic wearing a ribbon on his arm which was red in colour, and in view of the kind of work he was doing, I assumed that it was the sign of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, also as you told us in your statement, you didn't say you assumed it but you saw him actually with it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still think that it was the sign of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you say you knew Mr. Vasiljevic very well before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that I knew him especially well. We weren't especially intimate, but we were on good terms, good neighbourly relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would consider him a rather, you know, well-known person in town, wouldn't you? He was a waiter as far as we know, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People mostly knew him. Most of the locals knew him, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you are aware, he never had a bad reputation in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Muslims as well as Serbs alike didn't have any reason to dislike Mr. Vasiljevic, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you wouldn't know of any reason why somebody would lie about Mitar Vasiljevic, would you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you think there is any reason that people would want to lie about Mitar Vasiljevic if he was a rather well-liked person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the reason why some people said about Mr. Vasiljevic that he was a negative character. As far as I know, there was no reason for characterising him in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you consider Mr. Vasiljevic a friend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say basically yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would like to help a friend, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the reason why you came here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am here just to say how I know Mr. Vasiljevic, the kind of man that I think he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination? Re-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, just a moment ago when we went back to the question of the ribbon and when you -- your attention was drawn to the statement that you gave to Mr. Tanaskovic where the Red Cross was mentioned, the question was, in fact, to explain that. And you said that today you also think that it was the Red Cross sign. Now, I'm asking you the following: Do you think that for the reasons you stated a moment ago - and you said that it was a red band and that that is why you assumed that it was the Red Cross and because of the kind of function he performed, the post -- the job he was doing - or because you saw something else on it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, if you want us to take any notice of his answer, you must not ask leading questions. Just as in evidence in chief, you must not ask leading questions in re-examination. You've probably destroyed the value of his answer already, but I suggest that you do not lead him to the answer you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Well, there were several different answers so that I was in dilemma. I don't know what the witness's final answer was. So let me restate the question, rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'll read you his final answer. The question was:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, also as you told us in your statement, you didn't say you assumed it but you saw him actually with it; is that correct? And the answer was:

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still think that it was the sign of the Red Cross. Now, that's where he's finished. You may ask him any questions you like in a non-leading form about that, but that's where he is at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely that: "I think it was the sign of the Red Cross."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm asking you: On the basis of what do you assume that it was the sign of the Red Cross? What leads you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I actually saw - how shall I put this? - a red cross, an actual red cross, but the jobs he was doing, as far as I was able to see, would have been the kinds of jobs performed by somebody belonging to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that is sufficient. Another question asked by the Prosecution was the following, and it had to do with the function of Drago Gavrilovic. Now, I'm just interested in the following: Did he work Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the command that was at Bikavac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he come there, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice him up there, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there some other command in the town of Visegrad itself or at Bikavac itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was providing security for the command that was at Bikavac. As for the rest, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more question. I think that there was some misunderstanding how you started working on the 1st of April in the JNA. Did this come about because you responded to an advertisement published by the JNA with vacancies for certain posts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this advertisement, was it public? Did it appear in the public information media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could all citizens apply, all citizens of Yugoslavia, could they apply, the then Yugoslavia that existed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody who fulfilled the conditions of the competition or advertisement were eligible to apply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it for five work posts, five vacancies, and were all five vacancies filled after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a contractual relationship with the army, for which you received remuneration; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it have anything to do with doing your military service, that all able-bodied young men and citizens have to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, that is to say, from the 1st of April until the 19th of May, did you leave the warehouse at (redacted) or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VGD22 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions, but I do have an application before you excuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's regarding the prior statement of this witness. Under its present form, the only proper use, according to my understanding, that the Court can use it is to assess the credibility of VGD22. It is a statement that does contain an affirmation by the witness, and his signature, that he acknowledges, that he affirms that everything stated here is the truth. I would at this time tender that statement into evidence so that the Court can -- because of the importance of the issue raised, that the Court can use it substantively as a piece of evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But Mr. Groome, you can't bolster your witness' credit in that way. If there had been a suggestion of recent invention, you would get it in as a prior statement, but how else can it be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not seeking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not corroboration or anything like that. He's given his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not seeking to bolster any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You said you were putting it on the basis that it was relevant to credit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's before the Court as that now, so the Court -- the only proper use the Court can make of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not before the Court at all. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, the statements that are regarding it are before the Court. The only proper use the Court can make of it at this stage is to assess the credibility of this witness. My argument to the Court, or my application, is that given that it is a statement signed by this witness containing an affirmation that what's contained in here is the truth, and given the importance of the issue that it speaks to, I make an application to tender it into evidence so that the Court can not only use it to assess his credibility but also use it substantively to reach a decision on this important issue in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't see how that gets it into evidence. I'm sorry. What principle gets it into evidence? There's some independent evidence of what he is saying? Because he has told us what he has said. He's said a number of different things. We have to assess which one of them is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, then maybe there's a difference in law between my jurisdiction and the Court's. My understanding is that the statements made regarding this statement cannot be used substantively by the Court at this point. The only way the Court could do that is if it were to admit this statement as a piece of evidence in and of itself, and I believe there is a foundation for doing so, given that it's a sworn statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I have only been here for three years, but I have never seen it done. Have you got any instance where it has gone in independently of his oral evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not have any jurisprudence from the Tribunal itself. I do have a treatise on evidence, and I would be willing to raise the point or read the portion of the treatise on evidence, the legal principle upon which I'm relying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We have allowed statements to be used because they are hearsay, but only because they are hearsay that we think they have some value. A statement, a written statement such as that, is hearsay. It doesn't become anything better than that. Now, we have allowed hearsay evidence in because we are not restricted, as the common law would restrict us, to direct evidence. But I don't see that a hearsay statement as to what the witness said some time ago is going to assist us in determining which of the different versions he has given here is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would be my position, Your Honour, that it is not hearsay, because the witness is here in Court and can presently adopt it or has made an adoption of it in Court as something that was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you have no opportunity to have him do that. You didn't do it in cross-examination, as you could have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct in saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can see no procedural basis upon which you can get it in, and in any event, I don't see that it's not already in evidence. He agreed with Ms. Bauer that it was in his statement. Whether it was the same statement, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, thank you, sir, for coming here to give evidence and for the evidence which you gave. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to thank the President of the Trial Chamber for having listened to my testimony, by which I stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Domazet, while the next witness is coming, we were given this morning the document which was filed yesterday about this expert on X-rays. You haven't filed with the statement -- with the document the statement that he has made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And as you yourself was quick to point out in relation to Dr. de Grave's statement, you are entitled to have it 21 days in advance of his giving evidence, so just as the Prosecution is entitled to have this doctor's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know, Your Honour, but this witness, expert witness would have to take a look at the evidence in the Tribunal, which the Prosecution has, before stating his views. And I tabled a request to the Registry to that effect to allow him to obtain a visa for him to be able to come to the Tribunal. Perhaps he would need to have a talk with Mr. Vasiljevic as well and to take a look at all the documents -- or, rather, the X-rays that are relevant in the case. I see no other way of him being able to do this except if the X-rays to be -- were to be taken to Belgrade, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's something to that, but Mr. Domazet, what I'm concerned about is that this has always been an issue. It's been an issue ever since the case began. The Prosecution sought your client's consent to have him X-rayed sometime, as I recall, at the end of last year. Now, it's a bit dismaying that you are leaving all of the preparation of your case on this matter until now. I drew your attention to the fact that you had not put any expert opinion to Dr. de Grave when he gave his evidence, and you explained it was because you hadn't yet received a report. But at some stage, the Prosecution has to know what it is he's going to say, because as a result of what you did not do when Dr. de Grave gave his evidence, the Prosecution obviously has a case in reply, and it can call an expert to deal with your expert's evidence. Hopefully, though, the Prosecution will be in a position to be able to cross-examine your doctor based upon the report which it obtains from its expert as a result of the report that you have to produce. This is why experts' reports are specially dealt with in the Rules. The time can be shortened, and indeed I would hope that the Prosecution would cooperate in doing so. But nevertheless, before your doctor is called, they have to have the opportunity of obtaining advice from their expert as to what he says so they can properly cross-examine him, and then they will be in a position to call their expert in response. So you better work out how this is going to be done. If your doctor is going to come here and look at the X-rays and see your client before he gives his evidence, he may have to go home again before he gives his evidence. That's not the end of it. It's a very important issue in this case. I'm just, as I say, dismayed that it's all being left so late.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, two days ago I received another report from Mr. Groome. It is another expert opinion. So that that finding, too, seems to me to be considerably different than the previous one, and that too has to be looked at by my expert. So I will do my best. I will really endeavour to do what I have to do quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, may I suggest this: that you and Mr. Groome talk about some procedure that you can have. It may be that the two doctors can discuss the matter. I don't know. But we have not got an unlimited period in which to hear this case. We are all involved in matters that are meant to be beginning at the commencement of next year, and it was upon the agreed estimate, with some degree of addition added to it, that we undertook this case. Now, there's going to have to be something done between you and Mr. Groome as to how this evidence is going to be given and how the issue is going to be determined. But we cannot sit back and wait 21 days after your doctor has seen your client, had a look at the X-rays, had a look at this other report, which we haven't seen, and then bring him back and then call another doctor obviously in reply. So that's why I am raising it now, that you and Mr. Groome, between you, in accordance with the cooperation that you've so far been able to afford each other, can think of something, some way of getting around this. It is, as I have said, a very important issue in the case, and it's something which we cannot deny either party the opportunity of dealing with it properly and fairly so far as other party is involved. So during some adjournment, I urge you and Mr. Groome to come to some agreement or some proposal perhaps for us to consider so that the evidence can be given by both sides properly but after fair warning to the other party. Now, is the witness ready now? Right. Let's have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you please make the solemn declaration in the terms of the document which the court usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Your witness, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to introduce yourself? Tell us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: My name is Dragisa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please repeat your name and approach the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you properly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Lindo, Dragisa. Dragisa Lindo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you born, Mr. Lindo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: On the 8th of August, 1954.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live, Mr. Lindo?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could the witness repeat that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, you will have to speak up. It's very hard for the interpreters to hear you, and if they don't hear you, we don't hear you. So speak up, please. Now, where do you live, Mr. Lindo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Trsevine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Trsevine, I assume is a village. Is it close to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Trsevine is a village close to Visegrad, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lindo, in 1992 were you also living there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you working at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: You mean the company or what? Varda, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, before your mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: In the furniture factory Varda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about this period, that is, 1992. Do you remember at the time that the Uzice Corps was in town?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the period after the Uzice Corps left?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me regarding that period, after the departure of the Uzice Corps, where were you and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I was mobilised by the Territorial Defence. They established a kitchen in Prelovo, and I was there as an assistant worker. I would clean up and look after the hygiene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were working in this kitchen in Prelovo mostly doing maintenance of cleanliness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the people who were working in that same kitchen doing the same or similar work as you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes. There was the main cook, Vaso Vojinovic, his assistant Mitrasin, and this [redacted]. I can't recall his name. There was a health inspector who was there, Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him from before or did you meet him then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: We know each other from childhood. He went to school passing by my house. We went to the same school, and that's how we know each other. He completed his schooling as a waiter and went to Visegrad. So -- shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. So, Mr. Lindo, this Mitar Vasiljevic who is from Djurevici and who you say you know well was with you and with these other people, when the Uzice Corps had left, in Prelovo and worked there. Was he, too, mobilised like you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes. He was mobilised in Prelovo. He received a red armband. He took care of cleanliness and hygiene and the distribution of food and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he also responsible for supplies? Did he go and fetch victuals and other things that he needed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes. We had a small van which was mobilised by the TO, and it was used exclusively for getting food. What exactly were the foodstuffs, I don't know in detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, in addition to hygiene and cleanliness, he also went to fetch foodstuffs in this van which you had and which, as you said, had been taken by the Territorial Defence, probably from somebody, for their needs.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: It belonged to the Sumarstvo of which Vojinovic was in charge, the forestry company. I can't remember the first name now. Obren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this van was driven by Obren Vojinovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this van, which was really the property of Sumarstvo, this was probably a company of which Obren -- and Obren Vojinovic drove it, and they used this van to get supplies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So where did they go? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: From Prelovo to Visegrad. I don't really know exactly where they went. Where the front lines were. That was what it was intended for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Lindo, whether Mitar Vasiljevic wore a uniform, and if he did, could you explain what kind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic was issued an olive-green uniform such as the JNA used to wear, and most of us were wearing that uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the uniform that the reservists of the then JNA held at home? They were issued with them and they kept them at home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from what you told us regarding the duties of Mitar Vasiljevic, do you know whether he took part in the distribution of food?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: From time to time he would go, when these others were not available. This was according to a schedule, and I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally, did you go to carry food to the front line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could not have gone with him on such an occasion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember, Mr. Lindo, timewise, how long was Mitar Vasiljevic with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: He was there for about 10 to 15 days in this kitchen. After that, when the kitchen was to be moved closer, we went to the village of Blace, with the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you went with the kitchen towards Blace, was Mitar Vasiljevic with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how it came about that he was no longer in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Simply, we left. We went on working there. So I don't know. Whether he was mobilised to some other place, I don't know. I heard afterwards that Mitar had broken a leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood what you said correctly, Mr. Lindo, Mitar Vasiljevic stopped coming to Prelovo one day and you didn't know why.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
