utterances.text: And it seems to me that it's possible that he may have been reassigned to some other position but that you don't know about that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he was issued any weapon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't remember. He was naturally issued with a weapon. Whether it was an automatic, semi-automatic weapon, I really don't remember. But he rarely carried it, because there was no fire there. How can I put it? I didn't pay attention what kind of weapon he was carrying, whether it was automatic or semi-automatic. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, you know for certain that he was issued a weapon but you cannot now recall what type of weapon it was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those 10 to 15 days, as you said, that you remembered that he was with you, did you have any kind of problems with him or did anyone else that was with you have any problems with him, provoked by Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. I said we know each other since childhood. It's a good family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear later what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: As I said, I heard he had broken a leg. And then later I met him in town. I saw him with crutches. He had broken a leg. I don't know how much later this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination? Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lindo. I'm standing to your right, and my name is Mr. Groome and I'm representing the Prosecution in this case. I'm going to ask you a number of questions regarding some of the things you've testified about here this morning. From what you've told us, it seems that you were born the same year as Mr. Vasiljevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would it be correct to say that you essentially grew up together with Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. It's almost 15 kilometres away, but he had to go to school on foot - there was no bus - and he would pass by my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Vasiljevic attend the same school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As children growing up, would you and Mr. Vasiljevic ever play together?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: For the first four years, yes. I left school, but he went on to catering school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you can maybe help us understand a little bit about Mr. Vasiljevic as a boy. Are you aware of any particular hobbies that he had, perhaps sports, music, art, or horseback riding? Are you aware of any particular interest he had in hobbies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The town of Visegrad, did you know the names of or did you know who the Muslim imams were in that town?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: There are a lot of them. This was nine years ago. I never thought about these things. I can't remember. My friends -- I can't even remember the names of my friends now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I realise that it was a long time ago, Mr. Lindo, but if you could assist us and tell us approximately how many different imams would you say there were in Visegrad in the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't quite catch the word you're using.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lindo, I realise that it was a long time ago, but I'm asking you if you can assist us by telling us approximately how many imams, or Muslim holy men, lived in the town of Visegrad in 1992. Just an approximation will do.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with any of them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Among them? What do you mean? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Would you say that there were more than two Muslim holy men, or imams, in the town of Visegrad in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: You mean the number of them? I'm not able to tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, if you want to object, please say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I can be of assistance. The interpreter is using the word "imam." I would prefer the use of the word "hodza." Maybe the witness will understand it better. It is one and the same, "hodza" and "imam." The Serb population uses this term more often, and it's quite possible that the witness didn't understand the word "imam." If you ask him how many hodzas there were, maybe he will find it easier to answer your question. That is all I wanted to say. The same applied to Mr. Vasiljevic when that question was put to him. So if you could use the term "hodza," please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does that include the term "religious holy man," "hodza"?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so, Your Honour. A hodza is another word for the imam, but it is more frequently in use among Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Groome, I suggest you take up Mr. Domazet's very helpful suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I thank Mr. Domazet for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Lindo. That is what I'm asking you about: hodza. Let me repeat the question. Are you able to approximate for us about how many hodzas were in Visegrad in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I know of one only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I misused the word, or I used the other word, "imam," you said there were a lot of them. So were you thinking of something other than hodza when you said that there are a lot of them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't know what you meant. I thought you were referring to Muslims as a whole, in general, but I never heard of this word "imam." We use the word "hodza."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the hodza that you know, did he own a horse?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I can't remember now whether he had one. I really won't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a little bit about your work in Prelovo. How long did you work in the Prelovo area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: About all in all, from the time we were mobilised -- let me see. How long was it until the Uzice Corps left? After the Uzice Corps, it was. I can't remember. I didn't keep a diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to approximate for us how long Mr. Vasiljevic worked in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I said about 10 to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that Mr. Vasiljevic was -- I believe you said a hygiene inspector. Could you please tell us specifically what his function was? What would he do on a day-to-day basis? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: As I was saying, he would give us orders, the lower-level people. We were assistant workers. He was a kind of inspector. That's how I understood his position to be, because he gave us orders how to maintain hygiene, to make sure the food was clean, to wash up and clean up and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if somebody did not show up for work, would he be responsible for shifting people in their responsibilities to cover the responsibilities of the person who did not come to work that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything. People came regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: If perhaps one day you were sick, whose responsibility would it be to find somebody to actually cook the food, to do your job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Cook Vaso Vojinovic. He was the cook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. If Vaso Vojinovic was sick one day, whose responsibility would it be to find somebody to replace him for that day? Would it be Mitar Vasiljevic's?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: As he was a waiter he would do those things, but whether Vaso Vojinovic didn't appear for work one day, I don't know. It could happen, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question a different way. You said that from time to time, Mitar Vasiljevic would actually distribute the food, something different than his ordinary duties. What I'm asking is: Who would make the decision that on a particular day, Mitar Vasiljevic should not be in charge of hygiene but should go and distribute the food? Who would make that decision?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't remember, because I didn't distribute the food. So I was never close by to see people coming and going. I know that he would go to fetch food in the van. Now, whether they agreed amongst themselves who would do what, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the entire time that -- well, I'm sorry. I withdraw the question. You said that Mitar Vasiljevic worked there between 10 and 15 days and that from time to time he would distribute the food. Can you approximate for us how many times he actually went and distributed the food? Would it be more or less than two?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: The food was taken once a day, because for the evening it was dry-packed food so as to avoid travelling in the dark. So I really can't remember who went when. This school where we were working is a big building. I had my own premises where I was working, so I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the regular practice of your unit to distribute dry-packed food for the evening meal so that nobody would have to distribute food in the night? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose that was how it was. I don't remember any more now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a hypothetical question. In your opinion, had Mr. Vasiljevic expressed a fear of distributing the food because of where the location was? Is it your opinion that he would have been forced, nonetheless, to go distribute that food?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with that, as I said. I don't remember these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Lindo: During the 10 days or 10 or 15 days Mr. Vasiljevic was there, did you ever see anybody order him to go and distribute food against his will or against his reservation? Did you ever see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The place where you worked, where the food was prepared, did you yourself feel that under threat there? Did you feel that you could be harmed because of the nearby conflict, or did you feel safe in that place, in that school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: We didn't feel too safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you worked in this -- on these duties, was there ever an incident where somebody either in the school where you were cooking or somebody nearby was injured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't remember that happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your position, were you required to wear any special clothes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: It depended what people had on them. I had an SMB JNA uniform as it arrived, this other uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you required to wear that SMB uniform or that's simply what you chose to wear?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: We had it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, given that you've told us that the evening meal was provided as a dry-packed food, what time would you typically serve the midday meal and this evening meal? What time of the day would that be done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't remember that, because this -- the distribution depended when they got to it. We were cooking. Those of us who was in the kitchen, we didn't eat dry-packed food. I said that food was packed for those further away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what time was the kitchen expected to have finished the preparation of the midday meal? What time was that supposed to have been completed by?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, it depended. If you had enough wood and enough people to serve, then it was quick, but otherwise, I can't remember. I never paid attention to that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct in thinking that the food that you were preparing was for soldiers that were fighting on the front line? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, I didn't do the cooking. I was just one of the workers, assistants. So there was the cook, there were the other people, and I was in charge of the cleaning or anything that Mr. Vasiljevic told me to do, the hygiene, cleaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you again. The food that you were preparing though, the work of this team was to feed soldiers fighting on the front line; correct? You need to speak up so that the interpreters can hear you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would I be right in thinking that the commander of these soldiers expected his men to be fed at a specific time? Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what that time was? An approximation is fine. Is it noon, is it 4.00 in the afternoon, is it 6.00 in the evening? Can you give us an approximation of when those soldiers were to be fed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, it depended. It didn't have to be at a set time. I don't know. I never had to -- I can't tell you. I can't give you the exact time. I don't really remember. I don't know. It wasn't my ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you work there, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, the time I was there, when that kitchen started. Whether it was after the Uzice Corps, I don't remember. We were there in Prelovo. We went to Blace. How much time passed, I don't know. Perhaps more than 15 days. I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you finished your work for the day, how would you get back to your home?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I lived nearby, and he would go. Sometimes he had the kombi van belonging to the Territorial Defence. Well, he did what he could. He fended the best he could. I didn't actually follow all that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the "he" that you're referring to now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic. He lived in Visegrad. So he would go up to his home and come back in the van, or when Obren would go to fetch the foodstuffs or if he had to spend the night or the van had to spend the night from time to time. I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would -- would Mr. Vasiljevic sometimes drive down to Visegrad in this kombi van by himself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: He's not a driver. So nobody can take the vehicle. He's not a driver. He would have to be issued a vehicle. He's not a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said -- when you said "he had the van," meaning Mr. Vasiljevic had the van, did you mean that he had responsibility for the van and could direct the driver to go wherever he needed to go? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. No. No, no. I said for the transport, for transport to Visegrad. He went with Obren Vojinovic. And whether he went -- whether he ask an auto stop or stopped somebody along the way or -- he didn't have his own van. He wasn't a driver either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- you told us that you live close by to Prelovo. Did you ever stay overnight in the school?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. I'm from Trsevine. It's one village next to the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that Mitar Vasiljevic ever stayed overnight in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that one of the people who worked on this crew was a person by the name of [redacted] and that you don't know his first name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes, [redacted]. Whether [redacted]or -- I couldn't put him down on a list. I don't know the first name. It says [redacted] Whether it was 21 [redacted] or something, I don't know. So I couldn't mention it, because I don't now know his first name. So I couldn't state his -- I couldn't say Obren's name either a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you this: Is the reason you don't know his first name is because on this crew, people referred to him as [redacted]; that's what they called him when they needed to speak to him? 2 A. [redacted]was his nickname. [redacted]. I couldn't give you his name, but 3 [redacted]was his nickname. And [redacted], well, so that was without his first name, but his nickname was [redacted]. That's why I said it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe his physical appearance for us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, like me, a man like me, my sort of height. He had a moustache, like I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your height is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, is it 68? How should I know? I never measured myself. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he your approximate build or your approximate weight?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately how much you weigh?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Seventy-three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what was his approximate age?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't remember. He was from quite another village. He was there with me, but we never went into those things, about years and so on. And he lives abroad anyway now. I don't know for how long he's been living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he living abroad before his work in Prelovo, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. Yes, he did, abroad, and then during those - how shall I say this - mobilisation, during the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was from outside the Visegrad but returned when the conflict began and local Serbs were mobilised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would I be correct in assuming that Mitar Vasiljevic also would have known this [redacted]? It sounds like it was a relatively small crew. Would I be correct in assuming that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, whether he's abroad or not, I wasn't with him much, and I can't even remember his first name now. Now, whether somebody knows him or doesn't know him, they should have known, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking you is: The 10 to 15 days that Mitar Vasiljevic was there, at that time was [redacted] also working on this crew?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Were [redacted] and Mitar Vasiljevic working in this crew at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: [redacted] was there in the kitchen, but who did what, what responsibilities, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not asking you what their responsibilities were. I'm simply asking you: At the time that Mitar Vasiljevic was the hygiene inspector, was [redacted] working in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there any reason that you can think of why Mitar Vasiljevic, if asked to name the people he worked with, would not mention the name [redacted] as one of those people? Is there any reason that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the name either, so maybe -- that's what I'm saying. It was a long time ago. I don't remember. Maybe he didn't remember either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps. I want to ask you about the weapon now. You have told us about the weapon that you were issued. Are you able to say that everyone on the crew was issued a weapon? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, we were mobilised, so regardless of who we were and what we were, we all did, yes. Now, what it was, I don't remember. I know that I had a semi-automatic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you forced to carry a weapon? In other words, if you felt that you did not need your weapon on a particular day, could you be punished for not having it with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: It was a matter of luck. The guards were always there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you showed up for work one day and you had left your weapon at home, would those guards have punished you or reported you to the military police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, if for some reason you decided not to carry your weapon on a particular day, you could perhaps lock it in your house or some other safe place and not worry about being punished for not having your weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's correct that you would not be punished if you did not have your weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again if you could assist us with your experience. If somebody was caught misusing a weapon - let's say they were very careless with it or perhaps had fired it while being drunk - would the superiors in the Territorial Defence, would they take the weapon away from that person?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, it didn't happen to me. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any instance where a superior officer confiscated or ordered the confiscation of a weapon from one of the TO members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us: When did the kitchen move from this school in Prelovo to -- I believe the village is Blace? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I keep telling you that I really don't remember. It's nine years ago. Had I known that I would need that -- I never knew that I would have -- I would have noted it down, had I known that I would need it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what month it occurred in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, when you ask me that, let me tell you, I don't even know when the war started or when the war ended. I don't really know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me see if perhaps I can assist you. Are you familiar with the Orthodox holiday of the Holy Trinity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is: Do you know that holiday? Is that a holiday that --

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes, I know of it, but I don't know what month it falls in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the kitchen moved to Blace before the Feast of the Holy Trinity or after the Feast of the Holy Trinity? Are you able to tell us that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I keep telling you: I really don't remember. I don't know what month. Whether it was before, whether it was after, I really don't know. If I knew, I would say, but I don't know, and that's it. I don't remember, so don't please keep asking me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm just going to ask you a couple more questions regarding the time. You're not able to tell us, in other words, with any type of precision, when Mitar Vasiljevic left Prelovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: He was there a very short period, 10 to 15 days. He left, but what time and when that was, please don't insist. If I knew the dates, I would tell you straight away, right here and now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I see from your statement you've said that a few days after he left, you heard that he had broken his leg. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Several days. Now, whether it was a month, I don't know. It might have been a month. Whether it was a month or two. I said a few days. I meant some time later I heard that Mitar Vasiljevic had broken his leg. I was still doing my work and I had a lot of farming to do, and I didn't pay attention to any of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So but it could have been as much as one month or two months after he left that you heard that he had broken his leg; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, that's what I'm saying, but I don't remember anything. I can't tell you face to face even if it was half a year. I don't know. I don't remember. I never said a date. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time that you heard that Mr. Vasiljevic had broken his leg, would it be fair to say that you learnt that it happened -- that he broke his leg soon after he had the accident? It wasn't a long time, but a short period of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I said after a longer time, when he came back from hospital, I saw him in Visegrad with crutches and a plaster cast on his leg. Now, how much time went by, I really don't know. I can't tell you a date. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the first time that you learnt that he broke his leg?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I heard, a few days afterwards - I can't say - 10, 15. I didn't know how much time had gone by, but one or two months later I heard; I heard he had been in hospital and came to Visegrad, and I saw him in Visegrad and he was wearing a plaster cast and walking with crutches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear how he broke his leg?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, I heard what I heard, that he fell off a horse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know whose horse it was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us how it was that Mitar Vasiljevic came to be riding that horse?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I really don't remember any of that, what happened. He was immobilised. That's what I had heard. Now, what actually happened, I don't know. I don't remember. I wasn't informed about it. I also broke my leg. I know what it's like when you break a leg, because I myself have broken a leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, am I correct in thinking that when you first saw him after he came out of the hospital and you saw him with the cast, that one of the first questions you probably asked him was: "Mitar, how did you break your leg?" Am I correct in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you saw Mitar that day on crutches and with the cast, you never asked him how he broke his leg? Is that what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you did not ask him about how he broke the leg; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise --

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, also in your statement, you said that you know Mr. Vasiljevic well and that you asserted that he was not the member of any paramilitary unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness says, "No. No."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not believe that he was the member of any paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a person by the name of Dragan Tomic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about Pionirska Street. As you must know at this stage, this trial involves a house burning that occurred on Pionirska Street with a great loss of life. When did you first become aware of what happened on Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I really don't remember where the house burnt, what street. I tell you again, I really don't remember anything, because there was burning all over the place. So ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "burning all over the place," are you referring to the town of Visegrad itself or the villages surrounding Visegrad or perhaps both?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean the villages surrounding Visegrad and the town itself; correct? You need to answer --

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I don't remember when that actually was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm not asking you to tell us where it was or any details about it, but I'm asking you to recall for us the first time you heard that this occurred. When was the first time that you learnt of this event?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't remember. I really don't remember. Well, here I am, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can I ask you, did you learn about it in 1992 or did you learn about it at some point after Mr. Vasiljevic had been arrested and charged with it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn about it before Mr. Vasiljevic had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago that I don't remember when that Pionirska Street was or what house it was. I had my work to do, and I didn't go into town. I never went into town. I just said that when I went to town on business after a longer amount of time, I saw that Mr. Vasiljevic had broken his leg. Now, when that was, when that all happened, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lindo, I'm not asking you when the fire was. I'm just simply asking you when was the first time somebody told you that there had been this fire on Pionirska Street? Was it before Mr. Vasiljevic was arrested?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago I don't remember one, and I don't remember the other. I said I don't remember any of that. Whether it was May or December or -- I don't know. I don't remember any of the dates. I'm just talking off the top of my hat now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for keep insisting on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Groome, really. He's told you twice quite specifically he does not remember. Now, can you challenge that rather than just asking the question again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Don't you worry, sir. There has to be a limit to repetitive cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just that the answer is somewhat non-responsive, Your Honour, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is directly responsive. You have asked him:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: ... did you learn about it in 1992, or did you learn about it at some point after Mr. Vasiljevic had been arrested and charged with it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't remember that either. Now, that's clearly responsive and it's an answer to your question. Then you asked him again at lines 8 to 10 on the page, and he said:

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago I don't remember one and I don't remember the other ... I don't remember any of that. Now, that clearly is a responsive answer to your question, and there comes a time when you really can't pursue in asking him the same question again and again. You can cross-examine him as to his answer that he does not remember, but you don't do so by asking the question again. Well, we'll resume now at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before I begin, just to inform the Court, I have spoken to Mr. Domazet regarding the X-ray expert and arrangements to have copies made so that they can be sent to Belgrade hopefully within the next few days for that expert to see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're very grateful. Whatever you can do to make sure we don't have a long wait to get your case in reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: By the way, have you filed the other report that you have given Mr. Domazet or is it not for our sight yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- I believe there's no translation, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The transcript, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, actually the transcript is missing some of what you said, too. However, what you said was that you have made arrangements with Mr. Domazet to provide copies of the X-rays and reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And regarding the other report that Mr. Domazet referred to, the Prosecution received a report from another expert on Friday that was furnished to Mr. Domazet Monday morning. As it is not tendered into evidence, I think it may be inappropriate for me to discuss the results of it, but Mr. Domazet is aware of those results and can use them as he sees fit. And then just one other very minor matter. I'm going to ask the witness a number of questions regarding Exhibit D22. Because that's handwritten and because it's caused some confusion in the past, the Prosecution has typed up a copy of that list. With Mr. Domazet's consent, perhaps we can use the typed copy rather than the handwritten copy to avoid any further confusion. And I would propose that it be marked as Defence Exhibit 22.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That has only one set of numbers, has it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Have you seen this, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe you have, Mr. Domazet. This is -- I just did this over lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. It's new, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that will be Exhibit D22.1, and it will be under seal. Thank you very much, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that that now be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lindo, I'm going to ask you to look at Exhibit D22.1, and I'm going to ask you a number of questions about these people. But rather than us refer to them by name in court, I would ask you to refer to them, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. as I will, by their number that is just to the left of their name. Do you understand that instruction, sir? Do you understand how we will use that sheet of paper, D22.1, Mr. Lindo? You're shaking your head no. Let me give you an example. If there was a number 100 on that list and the person's name was Bozo, we would refer to Bozo as VGD100. Do you understand now how we will use this sheet? We need you to answer verbally for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it might be better if I explained to the witness. We're not asking you to learn them off by heart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] VGD20. I'm saying 20. I don't know it. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "VDG20, I don't know him," says the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're not getting any translation. We're still not getting any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear on this microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh. Somebody has been interfering with my microphone. It's on another channel. Yes. Anyway, I think the witness now understands that if we want to refer to VGD20, then we will refer to him by that number and not by that name. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] VGD21, I don't know him. Should I go right through the list from the top down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. Counsel is going to ask you some questions. If you have to refer to any of these people, what we want you to do is to refer to them by the number on the left-hand side - you needn't worry about the VGD; just the number - rather than by their name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first person I will ask you about, Mr. Lindo, is VGD7. Would you look at the name next to VGD7. And my question for you is: Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at the name next to VGD8. Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at VGD9. Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't know this one either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about VGD3?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about VGD4?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't know that one either. I can tell you straight away, I looked through this list briefly. I know [redacted] as a policeman here from this list, so you don't have to ask me further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that the only person you know on that list, sir? Don't mention any names; just the number. Is that the only person whose name appears on that list that you know the name of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think it will save us a lot of time, and we'll redact the reference to the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that if there was other evidence before the Court that some of the people, some of the names on this list which you do not recognise, were paramilitaries, would it be fair to say that you did not know who the paramilitaries were operating in Visegrad? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not know who the paramilitaries were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. I just know the White Eagles, that they came. I knew about them. They mistreated me a little. The man had his face blackened, and then I realised they were the White Eagles. That's how I learnt who they were, that they were the White Eagles. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after Mitar Vasiljevic stopped coming to Prelovo, would it be fair to say that you rarely saw him after that point in time? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago that I went to Blace, and after that I didn't leave for some time. And then after some time, I heard that he broke his leg. I told you that. And then after that I didn't see the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from between the time that the kitchen moved to Blace and the time that you saw Mr. Vasiljevic in a cast, on crutches, you did not see him during any time between those two events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are not able to tell us who during that period Mr. Vasiljevic may or may not have associated with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once again I want to ask you a couple of questions regarding something related to Prelovo. During your time in Prelovo, were you ever issued a red armband to wear on your arm, above your elbow? Did anybody ever give you a red armband?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No, not here on my arm, but on shoulders there were some kind of insignia. I can't remember which arm. Small ribbons. I can't remember the colour. Every soldier had them when they went to the front lines. And he had an armband over here, as I said, but I can't remember whether it was on his left or his right arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about what you had first. What you're describing you had, you wore on the top of your shoulder? Is that where you indicated you wore whatever it was you wore?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you affix that to the clothing or the uniform you were wearing? Would you pin it on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: One would tie it on, on the epaulettes. I don't know how to explain it to you. A tiny, little ribbon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you approximate for us about how long was this tiny, little ribbon?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Something like this, so you could tie it. Ten centimetres or so. You just tied it, knotted it there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you don't recall the colour of the one that you had. Did the colour change from time to time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: The colour did change, under their orders, from the orders of the superiors. One day it was one colour, the next day another, the third day another still.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what the purpose of this ribbon was? Do you know what the purpose was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: The purpose was to mark the troops - I don't know how to put it to you - so that other troops would not interfere, that it was all one Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the men on your crew that prepared food, would they wear the same colour ribbon as the men out fighting on the front line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I am afraid that even that I don't quite remember, whether they paid attention to this. Whether they changed it regularly or not, I really can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the cook, Mr. Vaso Vojinovic, did he wear a similar tiny ribbon on his epaulette? Did he wear the same thing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see Mr. Vojinovic with a red armband around his arm, just above his elbow?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what it was that Mr. Vasiljevic wore?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: He wore a broad red armband as a sign of the Red Cross, the medical, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody on your crew wear a similar armband with the red cross on it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Not with the red cross. For me, this red ribbon meant the Red Cross. But he carried -- the doctor would wear the red cross marking the medical corps. So for me, that is what the red cross meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Mr. Vasiljevic wear this every day when he went to work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your last answer -- well, I want to make sure that we're clear here. Was there an actual red cross on the ribbon -- I'm sorry, on the armband?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I told you that the red ribbon marked that it was the Red Cross. The red ribbon. And that is why I mentioned the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you again, and I'll ask you to answer with a simple question or no. Was there an actual red cross on this armband?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness -- or that the following Prosecution documents, document 102.1 and 102.2, I'm going to ask that a copy of that be shown the witness. I would note for the transcript that 102.1 is - I'd ask that it be distributed to the Court as well - that 102.1 is the English version of the original B/C/S version, which is 102.2. I'd ask that the second page be shown the witness, the B/C/S version, and that's 102.2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lindo, I want to draw your attention to the last -- July of 2000 and ask you -- I'm sorry. Did you give a statement to Mr. Tanaskovic, who is in the courtroom here today, did you give to him a statement regarding your observations of certain events in Prelovo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time you gave that statement, you realised or you knew that Mr. Vasiljevic had been arrested and that your statement might be used in a trial of this matter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was your sincere wish at that time to be as truthful as possible with Mr. Tanaskovic; was it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told Mr. Tanaskovic everything that you could recall about the events that he asked you about; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I draw your attention to the last line of your statement, just above the date, and ask you, does it not say: "I affirm that everything I have said here is true, and I am willing to repeat it in court"? I'd ask you, is that not written on the statement before you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I see the witness looking at the monitor instead of the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at the photocopy of the statement directly down on the desk.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I see. I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise Prosecution document 102.2, the document in front of you on the desk?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: This one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct. That one that you've just put your finger on. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature on the bottom of that document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And prior to signing that document, you had an opportunity to read it; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't quite remember, but I remember what I said, and I suppose I signed what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that a photocopy of the statement that you gave to Mr. Tanaskovic in July of 2000?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, the Prosecution would tender documents 102.1 and 102.2 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you going to put it to him at some stage as an inconsistent statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest that when you do so, so there can be no argument about the translation, you have him read the B/C/S version that he signed, and we'll get the English translation from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It might be a very good idea, too, if there was a copy given to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: They already have that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, right. Okay. Mr. Domazet, any objection to the tender of those two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: My only concern, Mr. Groome, is that we had got a whole system running of when an inconsistent statement is going to be relied upon that it's agreed that that's what it says so that we don't have a lot of unnecessary statements. Is it being intended solely for the purpose of demonstrating an inconsistent statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you want to run your argument about it not being a hearsay statement and it has some individual probative value?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That and -- it is both that, and it does -- I am offering it as impeachment. While I think the agreement that Mr. Domazet and I reached is a useful mechanism for saving time and we've employed it in every case up until this, I think in this case it is more appropriate that the actual document be put before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But why? Because I don't want now to have now a cascade of documents when their only purpose, and their only purpose is, as you say, is to impeach his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. I don't think that -- that is not my only purpose, Your Honour, and I assure the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can't see any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I assure the Court that there will not be a cascade of documents. At this moment, I cannot see the need to introduce any other document during the remainder of this case. I would propose at this stage that he only read the relevant portion. So I don't believe that will take very much time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. If there is no objection to it, they will be Exhibits P102.1 and 102.2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lindo, I'm going to ask you to simply read the second paragraph of your statement, and in the English version, it begins with the phrase "Sometime in April 1992." Can you find that paragraph and please read it for us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Not too quickly so that the interpreters can follow you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: "Sometime in April 1992, after the Uzice Corps had left from this area, I was assigned by the competent organ, I think I said the Territorial Defence, I was assigned to work in the kitchen. That was organised in Prelovo near Visegrad, which is about 20 kilometres from Visegrad -- from Visegrad. This kitchen was organised immediately after the departure of the Uzice Corps, because the people were upset, scared, and did not have food, so this kitchen was organised to feed the people, to assist, at least to some extent. In the kitchen I worked with Vaso Vojinovic and Mitrasin Glisic, and Mitar Vasiljevic was there too, as was [redacted]. I do not recall his first name. Vasiljevic was in charge of hygiene in the kitchen, and the food, and so on. He was a sort of health inspector, because he had an armband with a sign. It is the ribbon of the Red Cross. That is what I said, not that he had a red cross on it. Here, too, I said something like that. I didn't say he had a red cross; that he had this five- or six-centimetre-wide armband. He wore an olive-drab uniform, as I said, of the Yugoslav People's Army, and he had been issued a rifle. Whether it was automatic or semi-automatic, I really cannot remember now. I said that when I was giving the statement. In any case, he rarely carried this weapon, but I know that one had been issued to him, like all of us." Shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's sufficient, sir. Can I ask you: Who was it that first approached you regarding giving testimony here in Court?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Who was the first to approach me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: The attorney.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which attorney?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Rudomir Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from your own statement, did you have an opportunity to see any other statements in connection with this case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. I didn't know really what it was all about, whether it was so necessary. I knew the person, and now I've come here to tell what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to either see, or see a transcript of Mr. Vasiljevic's testimony in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. I don't have a TV over there. We live in the village. There's satellite now, and I don't have a TV set, and I work all day long, from dawn to dusk. And I just come here because you called me, and I'm making this statement here, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on your trip up here, Mr. Domazet told us yesterday that in the Sarajevo airport, a person working in a coffee bar threatened you and accused you of committing some crimes in Visegrad. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. No. Not me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who did this person, this waiter, accuse of committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: He accused - he didn't accuse - this one who was to come before me. They went to have coffee, and he mentioned my brother, how they knew each other. I don't know. And I said, because he was working in the police, and I know him, and this one was working in the police, and then this young man recognised him and asked him something, and he would complain to you and his turn will come. I -- what they actually said, I don't ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did this young man recognise?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid he mentioned the name, which we have protected here as a witness. I don't mind the witness telling you, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we've got the document, have we not, with the pseudonyms on it? He's got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Mr. Groome is asking who this young man approached, this waiter approached at the Sarajevo airport. This person is a witness here and he is due to appear as a protected witness, and this witness here doesn't know that. That is why I would suggest that we either go into private session or that he be shown the name in writing, and then he can say whether that is that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You're talking about VGD23, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, is there a piece of paper with that written on it? Yes. Put the name, would you? It's Witness number 14 on the list. Unfortunately, from our previous experience, I'm not sure that the witness will quite understand, but we'll try. Are you prepared to put the matter to him directly by the pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And then he can see from the piece of paper who it is you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, show that to the witness, please, and it will be exhibit -- it will be one of yours. What's your next number?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: 105, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you seen that, Mr. Domazet? Have you seen the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That is Exhibit P105. It is under seal. Show it to the witness, please. Now, sir, counsel is going to put to you a question about somebody to whom he will refer to as VGD23. The person to whom he is referring, his name is on that piece of paper which the usher is showing you. Please do not refer to him by that name. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the person who the waiter recognised? You need to answer verbally, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you present when --

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the waiter a person from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you know, what did the waiter accuse that witness of doing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I don't know, because they went on to complain, so I'm not familiar with the whole incident. They were up at the bar. What was going on, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything about that. That is why I said a moment ago that the man would be coming here and he will explain everything to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did Mr. VGD23 tell you for the rest of your travels, or during the rest of your travels, what it was the waiter accused him of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. We didn't have time for that, because we went on to the station for transportation. There were seven of us. There were three or four at one table, so we weren't all together. That was how the whole journey evolved. So he complained to Domazet, and I know nothing more about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lindo, you were given a guarantee, were you not, before you came to The Hague that you would not be arrested during the time that you are here? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. Nobody told me anything, nor did I think about it. When somebody's not guilty, I'm not afraid of anything. Why are you asking me that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there have been representations made that you did so require a guarantee that you would not be arrested. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lindo. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Domazet:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lindo, at one point, answering a question put to you by Mr. Groome about some paramilitary formations, you said that you only saw some people called the White Eagles and that you had some problems with them. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why I said that I had seen that, and they came and frightened me, and they had -- I was wearing a JNA cap, and they came with their faces sooted and I didn't know what they were. And he said if I don't wipe out that five-point star, he would take down my particulars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judging by what they looked like or judging by the dialect they were speaking, or their speech, could you judge whether they were from Visegrad or from Serbia proper?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No, I wasn't able to. I don't know them and I don't know them. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that your only contact with people of that kind?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your written statement, the one you gave to Mr. Tanaskovic and the one you looked at and partially read a moment ago, would you take a look at it again, please. And in the one but last paragraph, it says, and please look to see whether I'm reading it correctly: "I know Vasiljevic well, and I assert that he was truly not a member of any paramilitary unit and was not prone to killing and the like. As far as I know, he did not do that. He did not, no." Are those your words?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes, they are. And as I stand here, I can say and guarantee that he was not in any paramilitary unit. He was with me, and I say that on -- I guarantee it with my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That was, of course, not really arising out of cross-examination, but it will perhaps demonstrate to Mr. Groome why we don't have documents in evidence if we can avoid them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: "Paramilitary unit," not "military unit." "Paramilitary unit."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, possibly, but I feel that in Mr. Groome's questioning, when he quoted and asked the witness something precisely connected to that to say yes or no, the witness said, "No," meaning yes, because he said he was not a member. So it appeared that he was saying something else, and this was not clear to me when I saw the question and answer in the transcript. That's why I asked him again, to see if he stood by what he said here. I needn't have quoted it. Could have just simply asked him, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I admire you for that explanation. There was no doubt in my mind when the witness answered it just exactly what he meant, but still you got away with it. That's quite all right. We're not rejecting the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lindo, in answering questions put to you with respect to whether you knew Mitar and the schooling and so on, you said that for four years, you went to school together. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you weren't together. That's what I understood that you said, that you weren't together any more after that. So please say if so and why.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic, I said a moment ago, did go to the first four years of school, but he was from a better-off family, and he was better at school. And as you can see, he graduated from catering school, whereas I was poorer, and I wasn't as bright, and I didn't have the possibility. So I just did these four years and then started farming, whereas Mitar went on. When he finished school, he went into town. He got married. He got a family. So I know that very well. I know him very well as a waiter later on. And so there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally, have you got more than four years of primary school or not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: No. I finished four years, and I added on to that by taking some part-time exams to make up for the eight years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lindo, when you were answering Mr. Groome with respect to the type of work you did in Prelovo, you said in a way that Mitar was some sort of superior and that you would get instructions from him or he would tell you to do things. Was he a superior on that same sort of basis to others in addition to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, I said that he was the main person, because I was an assistant worker in -- dealing with hygiene. I cleaned up. So he was in charge of that and in charge of the kitchen, and of course, I saw to the hygiene. I had to see that the plates were kept clean and things like that. But he was the main inspector for me. He was the supervisor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean by that that as far as hygiene and sanitary conditions were concerned, he was the person that was -- that supervised your work and everything?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned someone with the name -- surname of [redacted] as being somebody who did something around the kitchen, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That person, did they go to Blace with you when you left?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they stay with you in Blace? And if so, can you tell us how long?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: He stayed in Blace, but I was reassigned. So I don't want to say why, but actually, I had broken a leg, too, when I was doing guard duty in Prelovo. Those were different conditions. I was transferred there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were transferred later from Blace; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereas the man [redacted] stayed there; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of work he performed there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, he was the assistant. He did the dishes. I did the firewood. He went to take round -- to distribute the food with the van, the same van that Obren Vojinovic drove. Supplies, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he drove the van.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Vojinovic, Obren Vojinovic drove the van round and brought in supplies for the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which one do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just once again to avoid misunderstanding. [redacted] drove the van in Blace and -- explain again, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: [redacted] was transferred to the kitchen and he worked as an assistance to Vaso, and then [redacted] began to drive around in the field, and then he went with Obren and he was the main supplier of food to Blace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you mentioned Obren Vojinovic, who drove a van in Prelovo and went to fetch supplies.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes, in Prelovo, and Blace, he was transferred to. But in Blace, the main one was for driving around the field, [redacted],. So he was the main one in charge there, [redacted]. He transferred to Blace, but Obren still kept driving. And Obren still keeps driving around today, too, that van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in Blace, this man [redacted], did he replace Mitar Vasiljevic doing the jobs that Mitar Vasiljevic did when you were with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Well, yes, but what he was actually called -- I know they went in the field, and twice a week they would bring in supplies. Whether he was the main driver or whether this [redacted] person went with him, I can't say now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The question, "Did he replace Vasiljevic or" -- yes. I must confess that your substantial cross-examination about this man named [redacted] completely went over -- the relevance of it completely went over my head, but if there is some issue to be raised about it, it is a leading question, I'm afraid, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is an absolutely critical issue in this trial, and I would be happy to point that out to the Court if it wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, at some stage no doubt you will, but it certainly wasn't apparent to me at the time. It's a leading question. It's been answered. I don't know whether you can do very much about it, Mr. Groome. You didn't object until he was well into the answer, I'm afraid. Mr. Domazet, I don't know how you can go about it. You can ask him in a non-leading form, perhaps, but I think that probably the value of the evidence is of little importance now, or little probative value, shall I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unlike Mr. Groome, I do not consider that this is of key importance, this matter regarding the man [redacted], but I wanted to ask the question because other people, and not even Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic, mentioned that particular person. And that is why I wanted to clear this up with the witness, because it does emanate from Mr. Groome's question. And from the answer, I understand that he was helping Obren Vojinovic and did what Mitar did. Perhaps that is why my question could have been considered to be a leading one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If the issue of the relationship between them is of importance, as Mr. Groome says, whether it's substantial or even minor, there is no doubt that the question is a leading one. Now, the problem is the weight to be given to an answer to a leading question is usually very little indeed. All I've done --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- you might be able to get an answer from him which is not leading which will have some value. It's rather difficult to imagine how it -- how you can. The problem, of course, is that the witness had well and truly started to answer it before Mr. Groome had got the interpretation and was able to object to the question. So I'm leaving it to you. If you want to try and get an answer from the witness which has some probative value, you can try it. I should warn you that the answer, if it becomes important, the answer which he has given cannot be given very much weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand, Your Honour, and I don't insist on further questioning in that regard. Let me just ask the witness one thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man [redacted], was he from the first days, that is to say, when Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic was in Prelovo, was he there, too, or not? Was he there from the start or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: He came in the last days. He was transferred to Blace with us. So he could have joined up in the kitchen, working in the kitchen, and continued to distribute and transport food with Obren to Visegrad. Well, he did come to get supplies in Blace. Now, at whose initiative or whatever, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dikic -- I'm sorry. Mr. Lindo, just one question in that regard. When you said he came in the last days before you went to Blace, is that right? Is that what you mean, before you went to Blace?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question for you: After everything you have told us, do you still state that Mitar Vasiljevic was the person who was with you in Prelovo up until the time when you say, 10 or 15 days later, he stopped coming? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGISA LINDO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask to be permitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you do this to every witness that you've cross-examined on?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The issue has arisen in the re --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What has?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The witness has mentioned that he broke his leg in Blace, and I'd like to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He talked about his broken leg in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He didn't say it was regarding Blace, though, Your Honour. There's a general reference to a broken leg, and it would have been irrelevant for me to have gone into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How is it relevant now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask him where he was treated and when he broke his leg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm still at a loss to know how this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
